utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Matthew Olmsted and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery for Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Before Mr. Olmsted begins, I would remind you, you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to continue where we left off yesterday in the disciplinary process that existed between April and mid-September 1992, but before I do, I want to clarify one answer you gave yesterday. Yesterday you mentioned that you were unaware of cases where the CSB chief did not authorise the initiation of disciplinary procedures against a police officer. Sir, was your role as disciplinary prosecutor such that you were informed about every decision the CSB chief made regarding whether or not to permit a disciplinary case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief could be aware of a disciplinary procedure if the immediate supervisor of that officer who committed the offence initiated the procedure. And I think that the chief never disregarded any such case or failed to initiate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I understand that's your view, but that was not my question. My question is: You as a disciplinary prosecutor, were you privy to every decision that the CSB chief would make with regard to a disciplinary matter?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had knowledge only of such cases in which I was involved as prosecutor. I was not aware of other cases managed by my colleagues. Nobody informed me of that nor were they duty-bound to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you remind us how many disciplinary cases did you personally handle that were assigned to you during this July through mid-September 1992 time-period?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three cases, and I believe that all disciplinary prosecutors had the same case load, that is, three, excluding Pile who probably due to the nature of his work did not take part. By "Pile," I mean Predrag Radulovic. And I believe that all the other prosecutors were charged with three cases each.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us during this time-period how frequently did you meet with the chief of the CSB to discuss disciplinary matters?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what about the CSBs -- the CSB chief's deputy chief, Djuro Bulic, did you discuss disciplinary matters with him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's return to the disciplinary procedures that we were discussing yesterday. Where we left off yesterday was that after the CSB chief authorised the initiation of disciplinary procedures against a police employee, the disciplinary case arrived at the disciplinary commission. And you explained to us that it was the commission's role to decide the case and impose a disciplinary measure. Is that an accurate summary?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like you to look at Article 297 of the Law on State Administration. This is 65 ter 10329. We can go to page 28 of the B/C/S and 107 of the English. And we're interested in the Article 297, which is at the bottom of the English, so scroll down a bit. Perfect. This article lists the following disciplinary measures which appears to be in order of their severity. First it lists reprimand, then it lists public reprimand, and then redeployment to another position for between three and 12 months. Next is a fine of 15 per cent of salary. And if we can turn the next page just on the English and go to the top. Yes. There's also mention of termination, which I assume would be the ultimate disciplinary measure. Mr. Rodic, were these disciplinary measures that the disciplinary commission could impose against a police employee during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Are there any other --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A reprimand and public reprimand were measures of -- imposed by the chief of the SJB for less-serious infringements. The disciplinary commission was not seized with such cases; it dealt with only more severe infringements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Other than the disciplinary measures that are listed here, were there any others available to the commission to impose against a police officer who has committed an act of misconduct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This article, 297, further states that: "Reprimand and public reprimand are usually pronounced for light derelictions of duty, while the measure of redeployment, fine, and termination are pronounced for severe derelictions of duty." Could you tell us for what types of violations was termination the appropriate remedy?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The measure of termination was most often imposed when the police officer committed a criminal offence or a severe type of misconduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you give us some examples of severe misconduct that wouldn't constitute a crime, but nevertheless would warrant termination?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can mention the failure to report for duty for three days in a row, then refusing to carry out an order, but that depends on the specific circumstances. Then abandoning the police unit at the front line, that is, going AWOL and similar kinds of misconduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were there acts of misconduct for which termination of an employee was essentially mandatory, that the employee must be terminated for what they have done?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us what those acts would be?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All severe dereliction of duty, do you mean some specific incidents or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, we won't go to specific incidents, but for instance a serious crime of murder or rape, would that be an instance where termination of the employee was mandatory?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: After the disciplinary commission has rendered a decision, how would the CSB chief be informed of that decision?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision of the disciplinary commission was dispatched to five addressees. One of them was the officer against whom the procedure was launched, the chief of the centre; then the chief of the finances section; and I can't remember the others. Anyway, there were five addressees, and among them there was also the chief of the centre. One copy went to the personal file of the officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: After the disciplinary commission has issued its decision, did the police officer involved have the right to appeal that decision?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where did this appeal go to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The appeal would go to the disciplinary commission at the second instance. It was at the MUP. It had four members who had deputies, and the second-instance disciplinary commission was appointed by the cabinet. I'm not sure what exactly it was called, cabinet of the Serbian republic -- I'm not sure what the official name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was that cabinet the minister's cabinet at the level of the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the second-instance commission -- well, actually the disciplinary commissions were autonomous in their work. They were independent. And the second-instance disciplinary commission was in the headquarters of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But we were talking about who appointed these commissioners and you said the cabinet did, and I wanted to clarify. Was that the minister's cabinet in Pale?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me explain. The prime minister's cabinet, the government, appointed the second-instance disciplinary commission, and the members were proposed by the ministry. The MUP services, first and foremost the personnel administration, selected officers who met the conditions to be members of disciplinary commissions. The most important criterion was professional training because not every professional was equally suitable. The most desirable persons were lawyers, and in second place there were people with a degree in the humanities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like to clarify a few additional issues with regard to the disciplinary procedures that existed during this April through mid-September time-period when the act of misconduct at issue was a police crime. First, if a police employee committed a crime and a criminal report was filed against the employee with the public prosecutor, was it still necessary to initiate disciplinary proceedings against that employee?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Criminal accountability did not exclude disciplinary accountability, or in other words, disciplinary proceedings would be taken up also.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In fact, it was obligatory in the case of a criminal act to initiate disciplinary proceedings against that police officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What about the reverse situation. If a disciplinary proceeding has been initiated against a police employee for committing a crime, was it still necessary to report that crime to the public prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the disciplinary infringement also constituted a criminal offence, then the disciplinary commission filed criminal reports irrespective of whether or not disciplinary proceedings were initiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, there was some error in the translation because the witness say the criminal police not disciplinary commission file criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Criminal, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, so to clarify that, it was the criminal police or the crime inspector police that would file a criminal report against a police officer who had committed an act of misconduct that constituted a crime; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the crime police who were charged with criminal offences. The disciplinary commission did not file criminal reports. It's not in the description of their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you explain to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what was the purpose behind this parallel system of criminal and disciplinary proceedings? Why institute both?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the criminal accountability of an officer did not exclude his disciplinary accountability. That can be found in the law too. If an officer commits a criminal offence on duty or off duty, the crime police would investigate it and parallelly a disciplinary investigation would also be launched because a criminal offence automatically constituted a disciplinary infringement also.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that's clear, but I want to get behind this and what's the policy reasons for this parallel system of criminal/disciplinary proceedings. Are disciplinary proceedings merely to punish the police officer, or do they also serve a preventative role within the police force?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a severe criminal offence was committed, the police officer had to be suspended. If -- in case of a serious dereliction of duty, disciplinary proceedings were launched because only the disciplinary commission could impose the measure of termination, and that was indeed done if a serious crime was committed. I hope I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Not quite. Let me try it this way. By disciplining a police officer who commits a crime, what message does that send to other police officers within the police force?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, unless I'm missing something, I'm not sure why you're pursuing this. Isn't it sufficient that the witness has said that, in fact, this was the procedure in the territory at the time. The historical reasons may be of incidental interest, but I'm not sure that it is of assistance. The witness has indicated that this, in fact, was the position. Need we go into the whys historically?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think so. I don't think it's a historical analysis. It's an analysis why there was both criminal proceedings and at the same time disciplinary proceedings, why both were important and what purpose the disciplinary proceedings served above and beyond the criminal proceedings. And that's what I'm trying to get to is you have this system in place where someone commits a crime, they're certainly going to be subject -- they should be subject to criminal proceedings but they're also subject to disciplinary proceedings, and I want to get behind that, and not historically but principally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We'll see where we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So let me ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: By disciplining a police officer who commits a crime, what message does that send to the police -- the other police officers within the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the message would be for them not to do these kinds of things, to put it in the simplest terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how does this disciplinary process benefit the reputation and public perception of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was two-fold. First of all, the public approves to see the MUP fighting unprofessional conduct among their own ranks, whereas on the other hand, they may be disappointed if they see the police officers committing such kind of acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And which were typically faster back in 1992, disciplinary proceedings or criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think disciplinary because we had certain dead-lines within which the proceedings had to be both launched and brought to a completion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what about the situation where a criminal case against a police officer was dismissed in the courts, for whatever reason? Could the police officer still be disciplined if the underlying conduct was harmful to the interests of the MUP; in other words, it constituted an act of gross misconduct nonetheless?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Irrespective of the case in point, the disciplinary proceedings would go on except in cases -- if the infringement itself is directly related to this crime, so if there is no such link, there is no proceedings; and that is the case today as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if a police employee committed a criminal act, under the reporting protocols that existed in 1992, who had to be notified of that criminal act?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that there was an obligation. I don't know according to the rule or instruction relating to urgent, regular, and extraordinary reporting. It provided the names of people who have to be notified. I think that when it came to criminal offences, even the minister's cabinet had to be notified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So if a police officer committed a criminal act, say down at the level of the police station, that information had to go all the way up to the ministry?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was this communication through dispatches, through which the chief of the public police station was informed, maybe the minister, all other heads of organisational units, just so to make them aware of the existence of such conduct and that they should try and do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What should happen to an SJB chief or even any other superior officer who fails to report to the CSB and to the ministry that a crime was committed by one of their subordinates, what should happen to that superior?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this system of communication through dispatches, I think that the original notification went from the duty operations officer to all these addressees, and then perhaps the public security station chief would then send a more extensive dispatch containing more details to the chief of the centre and the minister. If something like that happened out of working hours or during night, the duty operations officer would be informed and then he would immediately send a PD or some other type of dispatch to those to whom they're intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, but I want you to focus on the question that I asked, which is: A situation where a superior police officer fails to report a criminal act by one of his subordinates, in such circumstances what should happen to that superior officer? Should he be subjected to disciplinary procedures?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he would then definitely be committing a dereliction of duty, if his intention was to cover up the act.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what about a superior officer who refuses to provide information to his superiors about a criminal act of one of his subordinates. Would that also be subject to disciplinary procedures?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of such cases, but that would constitute sufficient reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: To whom within the RS MUP did the disciplinary procedures which you have described for us apply? In other words, who could be subjected to them?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Would that include reserve police officers?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were also subject to disciplinary sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what about members of special police units, were they subject to disciplinary procedures if they were, for instance, found to have committed an act of misconduct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Being MUP employees as well, that means that they were subject to the same procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like to give you a hypothetical. Let's assume that a reserve police officer was temporarily assigned to military duties. And while performing these military duties he committed one or more crimes. When the police officer returned to his regular police duties within the MUP, could he be subject to MUP disciplinary proceedings for those criminal acts?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it happens that a reserve police officer while on the front, that is probably what you referred to, committed a criminal offence, a criminal report would be filed against him, whereas a disciplinary sanction imposed on him would be to remove him from the war time assignment of the MUP and he would then be transferred to the war time assignment within the defence, which would then be followed probably by his being assigned to a military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And again, that would be pursuant to the disciplinary procedures which we've just described?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Would this be then done pursuant to the MUP disciplinary proceedings -- procedures that we've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be qualified in the sense that his job here with the MUP was terminated, because the fact that the other disciplinary sanctions could not be imposed on reserve police officers in the same way as they were imposed on regular policemen such as fine or transfer to other jobs, it meant that only the most severe sanction, which is termination, could have been imposed on them. That would happen the minute he was removed from the war time assignment in the MUP and transferred to the war time assignment in the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But did the military have the authority to terminate a police officer from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was a crime, a criminal report had to be filed, and the criminal proceedings will proceed regardless of the disciplinary measure that imposed to him. As to what happened later in the military, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think we're getting too far from my hypothetical. We're talking about a situation where a reserve police officer has gone to perform military duties. Now he's returned to the police force, he's back to his regular duties, for instance, as an SJB. And the question is: With regard to his criminal acts while he was performing military duties, could he be subject to disciplinary proceedings within the MUP for what he had done while he was at the front? And that is the hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness already responded by saying that he would be removed for the war time assignment in the MUP and that he would be transferred to the defence. That was the only measure applied to the reserve police officers. He already answered this question twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I don't think he has. I think we need to have it clear because we're in a situation where he's saying that in the military -- what the military does he doesn't know what they'll do, but we want to focus on what the MUP can do in that circumstance, so I just want to make sure the record is clear. So if I can have a little bit of leave here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- sorry, before the witness answers, the -- without addressing the objection articulated by Mr. Krgovic, I'm wondering how far you're going with this hypothetical because the assistance that the witness can give is in terms of what in practice happened. So the -- I would have thought that your hypothetical would have been limited to identifying the underlying principle and then you would have moved on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's not -- Your Honour, I see your point. But what I'm focusing on is the procedure, actually, aspect of it. I was actually going to ask him a question about what happened in practice, but right now I just want to establish the procedure. Someone goes to the front, they come back, it's known that they committed the crimes, would they be subject to the disciplinary procedures that we have been going through yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it would be easier for the witness and for the Tribunal if you would ask the question directly about the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll ask again, exactly what I just told Judge Hall. A reserve police officer committed a crime while on military duty, he comes back to the police force. At that point in time would he under the procedures be subject to disciplinary proceedings within the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Criminal proceedings have their own course. A disciplinary measure that would be imposed on such person would at any -- in any case would be to remove him from the war time assignment of the MUP. As far as I understand your question, that would be the answer. So that was a summary procedure. His military file would be transferred to the Ministry of Defence as part of the disciplinary measure imposed on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's as far as we can go on that. Now, are you aware of any police officers who were disciplined for crimes that they committed during combat operations in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to their committing crimes while on the front in the combat areas or in war?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm referring to committing crimes while on the front, engaging in combat activities.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any officers from the Banja Luka public security stations where I used to work committed any criminal offence of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What happened to the disciplinary procedures in mid-September 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mid-September, well at that time the rules that were in force back in April was still in force. Only if you were referring to the rules that were adopted on the 19th of September, 1992, relating to the declaration of general threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 1D54. I believe you're referring to the rules on the disciplinary responsibility of the Ministry of Interior workers of the Serbian republic under war time regimen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediate threat of war, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if you can look at the document that's on the screen. Are these the war time disciplinary procedures?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These rules were in force as of the second half of September until I think April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, and let's move -- let's advance one page -- two pages in the English, and I believe one page in the B/C/S. I think we saw on the cover page, but who issued these war time procedures?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of the rules were issued by the minister, so including this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And under these war time procedures, what happened to the disciplinary prosecutors and disciplinary commissions?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most striking novelty, or rather, the reason for the adoption was the introduction of a summary procedure. The chief of basic organisational units, i.e., heads of administrations and CSBs, were treated as the first-instance disciplinary organs; and it was the minister who dealt with the appeals as a second-instance disciplinary organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think you've already stated, but just to confirm. These war time procedures were in effect to -- until April 1994?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as much as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 2390.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, we've reviewed a few documents from this disciplinary case file, and this is the Ivica Gagula case that you served as disciplinary prosecutor on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was this decision, this -- it appears to be a decision on appeal, was this decided pursuant to the regular procedures or the war time summary procedures?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I believe in the -- in all fairness to the witness, the whole document should be shown to him if the question is such as my learned friend is posing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's a good suggestion. Why don't we turn to the next page in the decision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we see that the first-instance decision was rendered according to the previous rules that was in force until 19 September 1992, whereas the employee lodged an appeal because he was transferred to another job for six months, but since in the meantime new rules were adopted the second-instance decision was rendered on the basis of the new rules of the 19th December, in which the minister acted as the second-instance organ. And I think this was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we look at the last paragraph on this page it states: "In accordance with the provisions under Article 16 of the Rules on disciplinary Responsibility of Employees of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia under war time conditions, this decision is final and there can be no appeal." So this is an example of the minister himself deciding a disciplinary case under the war time summary procedures on appeal?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't look at it that way. As I see it, the second-instance disciplinary organ delivered a decision, and in this particular case that was the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. I think we're in agreement then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1288, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, when a request to initiate a disciplinary procedure was filed with the CSB Banja Luka, where was it recorded?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a request -- well, it is well-known to whom it should be forwarded. It should be sent to five addressees, to the disciplinary commission, to the employee in question, to the trade union for information only, and I can't remember who else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me be a little bit more direct so that you understand my question. When a disciplinary procedure has been initiated, is it logged somewhere, into some book or something?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretary of the disciplinary commission kept record of the proceedings. As I said yesterday, it was a technical service attached to the centre, or rather, to the personnel department within the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 2355.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a hard copy of this log-book for the witness to refer to. It's going to be easier so he's not having to flip back and forth on the computer screen to look at things. And I apologise, I should have gotten a hard copy for the Trial Chamber as well. Just so you know, the English translation is only a partial translation. It translates the portions of the log-book that I will be discussing directly with this witness. It's quite a large book, as you can see, so I didn't want to burden our translation staff with that project.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the log-book that's in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is, in fact?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a log-book of disciplinary cases with the CSB of Banja Luka for the period from 1992 through 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge was there any other log-book at the CSB Banja Luka in which police disciplinary cases were recorded during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can look at page 23 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, sir, I have handwritten in the top right-hand corner page numbers that correspond with our documents on the computer screen to help you find it. And perhaps I've gotten the numbers wrong. We'll see. Yes, I've got the numbers wrong --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I've got the numbers wrong. Let's turn to the next page, page 24. And in the English it would be page 2. Sir, according to this log-book, which is the first disciplinary case filed after the creation of the RS MUP in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the disciplinary -- the first disciplinary case? Because I heard you say "criminal," but I think you meant disciplinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I meant disciplinary cases.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was received on the 23rd of April, 1992, for an event that took place on the 13th of April, 1992. Zeljko Bursac and Robert Barusanin were reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is entry number 3 on this log-book?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, and we'll kind of go through, but -- we don't need to go through each one necessarily, but can you tell us what kind of information is contained in the various columns of this log-book.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the first column you'll find the number, then in the next column there's a name and surname of the employee against whom the procedure is initiated. In the following column the date of the violation, then further to the right the date of receipt of the initiative and request, then the date of submission of the file to the prosecutor, then the number under which the request was logged, then the name of the president of the disciplinary commission, then there is the qualification of the violation, then whether there was an appeal and if so on which date. And the following column -- well, I can't make it out -- well, of the date and place of the hearing in chief. Then the decision or disciplinary measure, its type and severity. Then the record number of the decision and what it was served to the parties.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please go back. We haven't caught everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, can you pause there. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. There's a technical problem. What the witness is reading is -- cannot be seen on the screen, so it's difficult to follow. It's probably on the following page of the document because the last part of what you have read out was not visible on the screen. Now it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very good. Let's see where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But perhaps we could just be more general because I think the Trial Chamber can read the headings themselves. The second page dealt with the hearings as well as the appeals process in the disciplinary measures. Is that what it does?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we return to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the eighth column contains a couple abbreviations, and in particular it refers to a ZOUP, and if we look down along the eighth column - we want to scroll a little bit over in the English and the B/C/S. There for the English and there for the B/C/S. It refers to ZOUP, and then if you look down what it does it refers to this Article 114. Can you tell us what law this is referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That column contains the qualification of the infringement, and ZODU stands for Law on State Administration, although I believe that this is not the correct acronym. But the secretary of commission -- of the commission used it; whereas, ZOUP stands for Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to testifying here today, you had the opportunity to review this disciplinary case log-book for 1992 through 1997, and we also asked you to compile some statistical information from this log-book. And I'd like to ask you some questions about what you were able to find. Based on your review, what was the total number of disciplinary cases for acts of police misconduct which occurred between 1 April and 31 December 1992 according to this log-book?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the time-period from the 1st of April, 1992, through the 31st of December, 1992, according to the records I had a chance to review, I found out that there was a total of 27 disciplinary proceedings against 32 police officers in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Out of those 27 cases, how many of those cases involved Serb police employees?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of that total number, 17 disciplinary proceedings were launched against 22 police officers of Serb ethnicity for serious derelictions of duty. It is possible that in one or two cases I may have made a mistake because Croats and Serbs can have similar names, but I don't believe that the mistake -- or the margin of mistake goes beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So am I correct to assume that the remaining ten or so cases against police officers were cases against either Muslim or Croat police employees?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just so we're clear as to what your statistics include, do they include disciplinary cases processed under both the regular procedures as well as the war time summary procedures?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do they also include disciplinary violations that occurred in 1992 but weren't processed until 1993 or later?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to review these 17 cases against Serb police employees that you've identified. But before I do, were you asked by the ICTY Office of the Prosecution to assist in tracking down the files for these disciplinary cases before testifying here?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you entirely successful in that endeavour?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Why not? What happened to these case files?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it was a crime police of the crime police administration of the RS MUP who collected those files. I was involved too. In 2006 these disciplinary case files were destroyed pursuant to an instruction on archiving those files. For such files the stipulated period of keeping them is five to ten years, but that does not apply to the log-book itself. It is kept permanently, and I indeed found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So let's return to this first disciplinary case, the one against Zeljko Bursac and Robert Burusanin, as it's listed as entry number 3 --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it's Barusanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Maybe if we can scroll a little bit over to the left in the -- yeah, there we go. Same thing -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us what the ethnicities of these two police employees were?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that Zeljko Bursac is a Serb. I suppose that Robert Barusanin is a Serb too, but he could also be a Croat judging by the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what police station were these two police officers from?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Bursac was a police officer of the Ivanjska police station not far from Banja Luka, whereas Robert Barusanin worked at the Centar police station in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What disciplinary offence did they allegedly commit, these two police officers?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were charged for murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the ethnicity of the victim was?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The victim was Djuradj Knezevic, and I believe that he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the outcome of these disciplinary proceedings? And if you have to refer to the log-book, please do.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The outcome of the disciplinary proceedings was termination of service for both of them. Zeljko Bursac appealed the decision, but the appeal was refused and the initial decision was confirmed, and that is termination of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When -- what date was their employment contract terminated or at least the decision to terminate their contract made?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th of October in the district court in Banja Luka where they were in custody, a disciplinary hearing was held on that day, and I suppose that it was then that the first-instance decision on the termination of service was passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So on the date of the decision of their termination, they were being held at the district prison, would that be the Tunici [phoen] prison?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because both -- the -- they were subject to disciplinary proceedings and parallelly to criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So a criminal report was filed against these two police officers with the basic -- or the public prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the result of their criminal case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their criminal case had as an outcome that Zeljko Bursac was sentenced to 11 years in prison and Robert Barusanin to four years and six months in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, let's move -- let's go back one page and go to the next case listed on this page, the log-book page, and we see it's a disciplinary case against Slobodan Maksimovic. Who was his -- what is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall what SJB or what organisational unit within the police he worked for? And if you don't know, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at the column that describes the articles under the law on internal affairs and Law on State Administration that he was charged with. If we can scroll over just a little bit on the computer screen. There, yes, on the B/C/S and the English. Perfect. Now we see under column 8 that Maksimovic was not charged under Article 296, paragraph 2, item 1 of the Law on State Administration, which as we saw before, was the provision regarding disciplinary violations for committing a criminal act. He was not charged with that, so what does this tell us about his disciplinary violation?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, under Article 114, paragraph 1, item 9 of the Law on the Internal Affairs, and that referred to conduct that was detrimental to the reputation of the ministry. His violation could not be put under a heading of -- that was to be found in the Law on State Administration, so a provision of the Law on Internal Affairs was chosen instead. That was not the only such case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So his offence was not a criminal act according to this log-book?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could have been. I cannot tell based on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that's where I was going with this and maybe it's just a step of logic. But if you look at the case above it, the one that we've just talked about, they're charged under this Article 296, paragraph 2, item 1, of the Law on State Administration. And we saw that that is the provision that dealt with criminal acts by an employee. But we see Maksimovic is not charged with that. And what I was asking you is whether that would imply that he was not being disciplined for a criminal act.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's move to the next case on this page, which is against Zeljko Stupar. What was his ethnicity, or what is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what disciplinary violation did Mr. Stupar commit in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He committed a criminal offence. He smuggled weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at P1002. And this appears to be -- well, it's labelled a telegram, and it's to all SJBs, and it's coming from the CSB. If we can turn to the -- and it's dated 30 April 1992. And if we could turn to the second page of I believe it's just the English. On the second page it states that: "At Kljuc SJB it was established that active-duty policeman Zeljko Stupar had sold and smuggled a certain number of fire-arms and a quantity of ammunition, thus committing a criminal offence." Is this the crime for which Mr. Stupar was submitted to disciplinary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was both a criminal and disciplinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Are you aware whether he was -- whether criminal charges were filed against him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we look at the next paragraph it discusses the murder committed by SJB Banja Luka police officers Robert Barusanin and Zeljko Bursac in the Prijedor area. Is that the disciplinary case that we discussed or we talked about earlier?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's move -- let's go back to the log-book, the previous exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, it's 10.25. Would this be a convenient point to take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It would be a very convenient time, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So let's resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: While we're on this document I might as well ask you, this case against Zeljko Stupar, do you recall the facts of this case, in particular, to whom he was selling the weapons?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's go back to -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a police officer at the Kljuc SJB. He was not in Banja Luka, so I'm not familiar with the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let's go back to 65 ter 2355, which is the disciplinary log-book. And if we can go back to page 2 of the English and basically the page you're on which is technically page 24 on e-court. And we can see the next case after Zeljko Stupar is a case against Zeljko Vukovic. And we can see from column 5 that you are mentioned there, Radomir Rodic. Does that mean that you were disciplinary prosecutor for this case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what police station was he from?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skender Vakuf, which today is called Knezevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was his disciplinary offence back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case the grounds for initiating disciplinary proceedings against Zeljko Vukovic were not a criminal -- it wasn't a criminal offence. It was a dereliction of duty. In a short time-period he committed three severe instances of dereliction of duty. In late March 1992 he reported to work drunk, then in early April 1992 at a traffic check-point he shot at a traffic sign and destroyed it, and then in early May he sat in an official vehicle and abandoned his official work-place without permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was the outcome of his disciplinary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could tell from the records, the sanction imposed was a deduction of 15 per cent of his salary for six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to the page 4 in the English version of this log-book, and it will be the next set of entries in the B/C/S version which begin on page 26. Mr. Rodic, we see on this page the next six entries in this log-book. Could you tell us which of these disciplinary cases were against Serb police officers?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this page I would say that only the entry or entry number 11, Milutin Buksa who was a police officer at the time was the only Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what police station was he from?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in charge of traffic safety in the police station in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was his disciplinary offence? What was his act of misconduct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was processed disciplinary --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, if you could just stop and maybe start again because the interpreter missed the date. If you could just explain again what was the disciplinary offence.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will. His disciplinary offence or proceedings were conducted due to an act that he committed on the 16th of June, 1999 [as interpreted], at the check-point where he worked together with another six reserve police officers and two military police officers from a citizen who I believe was from Knin confiscated unlawfully 15 kilogrammes of coffee and distributed it among themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was -- what was the ethnicity of the citizen who they took the coffee from?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of Mr. Buksa's disciplinary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just before the witness answers, line 12 says 16th of June, 1999, I believe it was 1992. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, just to clarify the record, the disciplinary offence at issue which Mr. Buksa was involved in, that occurred on -- in June 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of Mr. Buksa's disciplinary proceedings. And the information may be on the next page of the log-book.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have just turned the next page. He was fined by 15 per cent of the net salary in the previous three months -- received in the previous three months and to be applicable in the next six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next page in the log-book, page 28 of the B/C/S version and page 6 of the English. Now, we see on this page entry number 14, the Ivica Gagula case. That's the case that we have been talking about -- looking at a few documents about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us on this page which of the police officers were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under number 13, I think that Drago Serval was a Serb; and number 17, Petar Tanazovic and Zoran Davidovic; and number 18, Slobodan Miljus.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We can see -- let's first turn to Drago Serval, and we can see from the fifth column that your name is mentioned there. Does that mean that you were disciplinary prosecutor for that case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What police station was he assigned to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police station centre in Banja Luka; however, I'm not quite sure whether he was a Serb or a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do you recall what his disciplinary offence was?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serval was subjected to disciplinary procedure because on the 29th of July, 1992, he was given a day off from the unit that was somewhere on the front line, but he failed to return over the next few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was the outcome of his disciplinary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the disciplinary proceedings, Serval asked for an agreed termination of service, if I remember correctly, but I also see from the documents that he lodged an appeal against the original decision that was probably relating to termination. And I see that his appeal had been rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could we move to the previous page listing the names of the cases, so back to page 28 of the B/C/S and 6 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And let's look at the next case against a Serb police officer that you identified, which is entry number 17. Could you tell us who were Peter -- or Petar Tanazovic and Zoran Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petar Tanazovic was deputy commander of the Majdan police station in Banja Luka. Zoran Davidovic was a police officer in that same police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was their disciplinary offence?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They committed a criminal offence and were subjected to disciplinary procedure because on the 23rd of September, 1992, Petar Tanazovic at the check-point in the village of Vrbanja in Banja Luka killed a reserve police officer from the station Bosko Kavic. Zoran Davidovic was with him, but he did not prevent him from committing that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the ethnicity of Bosko Kavic was?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosko Kavic was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was the outcome of their disciplinary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Termination of service. I think that Davidovic filed a complaint to the second-instance disciplinary organ, but it was rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And were they also subject to parallel criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The security services centre filed criminal reports against them to the district prosecutor's office in Banja Luka. Petar was sentenced to 14 years in prison and he was released recently -- actually, two or three years ago, while Davidovic was sentenced to two or three years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very well. We'll talk about entry number 18, Slobodan Miljus in a little bit. But if we can turn -- yes, turn back to that -- the previous page, page 26 -- or, I'm sorry, 28 of the B/C/S, 6 of the English. Can you tell us according to this log-book what happened procedurally to the cases against Tanazovic, Davidovic, and Miljus? And perhaps while he's doing that we could scroll a little bit over in the English. Yes. It says: "File returned to the submitter of the initiative of the procedure," ... et cetera, et cetera. Could you explain what happened with those cases?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since the event took place in those days when the new rules on disciplinary liability in war time came into force, the disciplinary prosecutor or the official who distributed files to disciplinary prosecutors did so. But as I said, since those days the new rules came into effect the case was returned to be processed according to the new rules rather than the old ones. It was returned to the commission's secretary, and in this instance, it was acted according to the new rules in which the chief of the centre was the first-instance disciplinary organ and the minister was the second-instance disciplinary organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn now to page 30 of the B/C/S, and we don't have an English translation of this page. And, sir, if you're looking at the numbering at the top it's page 29 for the numbering I gave to it, but just add one number to all my numbers. Essentially it's just the next page. I'm sorry, the next page after that. So we see that the log-book jumps from 1992 with the initiation of the war time summary procedures and it goes to 1994 -- in fact, it's going to April 1994. Why does it do that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me why we have 1992 and then 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. What was happening between September of 1992 and April of 1994 that we're jumping ahead to 1994 here?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This looks a bit confusing, but I think that the reason for that is because the secretary of the commission who kept the records, and in my view he did that for economical reasons because I don't know if you know that in that period the police stations and the centre and the Ministry of the Interior, there was an enormous shortage of stationery. And you can see if you look at the beginning of this log you can see that this was kept in the books that were envisaged to be used for persons remanded in custody. So we had to adapt these books. Maybe you will find it difficult to understand that, but we didn't even have pencils, let alone all these proper books and records. Therefore, I think that the commission's secretary used every blank paper to keep the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I might interrupt briefly, Mr. Olmsted, I just wish to note for the record that the accused Zupljanin is now present in court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When we flip ahead some of the pages, let's go to page 54 of the B/C/S and page 8 of the English, and, sir, if you could just flip through the pages. We have 1994, the first entry being April 1994, and then we flip through the pages and we get to this page, page 54 of the B/C/S, and it jumps back to 1992. Under which procedures -- some of these cases look familiar. Under which procedures were these disciplinary cases processed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to this I would say that these procedures were finalised according to the new rules that were in force during an imminent threat of war. Some cases were started according to the previous rules, but also recorded are the cases that were finalised according to the new rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And why don't we now flip ahead to page 56 of the B/C/S and page 10 of the English. And here we see that after 1992 we go to 1993. Can you tell us, are these the disciplinary cases processed in 1993 under the war time disciplinary procedures?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now why don't we flip ahead to page 72 of the B/C/S. We don't have this in the English translation, but it's self-explanatory from the heading, I think. And here we see 1994, and we have entries beginning January 1994. And if you just flip ahead from the pages from that point, can you tell us whether these are the disciplinary cases that were processed under the war time disciplinary procedures up until the time that the RS MUP returned to the regular procedures in April of 1994.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, why don't we do that.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can see that these are the records of disciplinary cases - rules on disciplinary liability of MUP employees during a war time regimen, which means that they were conducted according to those specific rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that near the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think if you flip ahead through these pages of the log-book, eventually you will return I think to 1995 or you will advance to 1995 under the regular procedures. But let -- let's see if we can explain this log-book because I think you're right that it is a bit unusual because it's a bit out of order. But tell me if this is possible here. We have the log-book for 1992 and then up in September we have the new war time procedures. Then the log-book goes to April 1994, which is where the regular procedures were implemented again. And then we go back to 1992, 1993, and 1994 and we see the cases from the war time procedures. Is that an accurate summary of what we've just looked at?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this precisely confirms what I said earlier about the secretary of the commission. We saw different handwriting in 1992 and in other years, which means that there was a new secretary of the commission whose task was to keep this log-book. He did that in order to save paper as much as possible because nobody could provide stationery for us at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's return to page 54 of the B/C/S, which is page 8 of the English. And these are the war time disciplinary cases from 1992. And, sir, if you could tell us which of the disciplinary cases on this page were against Serb employees who committed disciplinary violations between the 1st of April and the 31st of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have Petar Tanazovic, Zoran Davidovic, Ljubisa Nikolic, and others - it doesn't say who the others are, then we have Slobodan Miljus, I think that Zoran Vukojevic was also a Serb, Dusan Pasic, and Sasa Maksimovic. Shall I go on, or shall I stop here on this sheet?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, stop there. And if we can look at Sasa Maksimovic, what was the date of his act of misconduct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to go back --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, maybe I can help you, if you can look at column -- if you look --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it says the date when violation took place, 21st of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. We won't focus on that one because it's before April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you could look at entries 3, 4, and 6, are these the same cases that appeared earlier in the log-book that we've already talked about?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Petar Tanazovic, Zoran Davidovic, and I also think that refers to Slobodan Miljus, but let me check. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So we've already talked about the case of Tanazovic and Davidovic. Can we turn to Slobodan Miljus, and could you tell us what disciplinary offence he allegedly committed.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Miljus committed a criminal offence. On the 11th of November, 1992, he falsified identification paper for three non-Serbs, while the Sanski Most public security station had filed criminal reports against those three individuals for the crime of armed rebellion. After providing false IDs for them, Miljus drove those three individuals to the UNPROFOR base in Dvor in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What police station was Mr. Miljus from?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from the Prijedor public security station. I don't know which police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall what the outcome of his criminal proceedings were? If you don't know, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His service was terminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, that was his disciplinary proceedings. What about his criminal proceedings? Perhaps you didn't follow them, but do you know was he eventually convicted of his crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, the entry above Miljus we have Ljuban Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubisa Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct. I did it wrong. Now, he was -- he has a similar classification number to Miljus. Was this the same disciplinary case or a different one?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was a different case because he was a member of the police station or the public security station Gradiska. And I believe that these two cases are totally unrelated. If there is something that might lead one to such a conclusion, it might be ascribed to a mistake made by the commission's secretary because I cannot see any link between the two offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Then we have under entry number 7 we have Zoran Vukojevic. And if we look at the next page, could you tell us what was the disciplinary measure imposed against this police employee?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A fine amounting to a deduction of 15 per cent of his salary, but there is no specific time-period during which this punishment was to be imposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Let's return to the previous page. And the next entry, entry number 8, is Dusan Pasic. Can you tell us what was this police officer disciplined for in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusan Pasic worked at the Bihac SJB, which was relocated to the village of Ripac near Bihac. On the 29th of November, 1992, he, with another active-duty police officer and 18 reserve police officers, refused to carry out a task after which a disciplinary sanction was imposed to the effect that his service be terminated. He appealed but the appeal was refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you explain in more detail what task he failed to carry out. Was it failing to report to duty or report to war time assignment?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know the police went to the front line like other citizens did, and that was also a work duty of ours. And he refused to go to the front line - I don't know exactly where - together with the others. They refused, and he was subject to disciplinary procedure, and the other police officers were taken off the war time assignment schedule of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 56 of the B/C/S, page 10 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And these are the, as we've talked about before, the 1993 disciplinary cases that were processed under war time procedures. And we see I think ten entries, but can you tell us based on column 4 how many of these cases on this page involved acts of misconduct in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your question fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sure. I'll repeat it then. If you look at column 4 you see the date of when the violation took place, and you see some dates are in 1993. Those for the purposes of your testimony I'm not interested in. I'm only interested in the ones from 1992, and can you tell us which ones -- which entries are for violations that took place in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the column with the date when the violation was committed there are some cases where the violation was committed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, and could you just -- for the record could you provide those numbers, entry numbers.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the register for 1993 you want me to enumerate the cases which have to do with the violations that were committed in 1992? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Exactly. Could you just give us the entry numbers.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1, Drago Letic, date of violation 4 October 1992; then Nura Hodzic, 7th of December and 30th of November, 1992; then Drasko Acic, 10 October 1992; then there's Petko Djukic, 1 October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then there is Zeljko Vukojevic, 14 May 1992; Djuras Bosnjak, 31 December --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, let me stop you there. Let's just focus on this first page. We'll go to the second page in a bit. I think you've identified entries numbers 1, 2, 4, and 10. Could you tell us of these four cases which were against Serb police officers out of these four?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Letic may also have been a Croat. Nura Hodzic is not a Serb. Drasko Acic is a Serb. Petko Djukic is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the four cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. And let's go -- let's just -- let's talk about Drago Letic. I know you're not certain whether he was a Serb or a Croat. You mentioned he committed acts of conduct in -- misconduct in 1992. Did he also engage in misconduct in 1993 as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 4 October 1992 and 26 January 1993. He worked at the Teslic SJB. I don't know him at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, we appreciate the evidence that has been offered by this witness in respect of the disciplinary procedures that were taken in response to offences committed by servicemen of the MUP. I think you've made your point, that we have now received a pretty good idea of how it worked and what the offences were and how they were handled. And so I'm wondering how much further down this line do you wish to go? And I'm asking of course in respect of the time that you have asked for. I think you indicated that you would seek to reduce the time that you had actually asked for. And so if these considerations are still possible, then I'm just curious to know how further you wish to pursue this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I do want to go through -- he identifies 17 cases against Serb police officers, and I do want to go through them. And I'm trying to do it as quickly as possible just to give an understanding of what those offences were so that we know about the entries in this log-book because this is the log-book that covered the time-period of this indictment. I will endeavour to go much faster, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do we need to go through all 17 of them? Is that really necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I think so because I think we need to understand what the offences were, whether they fall within our indictment or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would assume that the picture that is emerging from the cases that we have gone through is pretty consistent, and so is there anything new coming out of the remaining cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure the Defence is going to stipulate that all these cases -- these 17 cases do not fall within our indictment. So I think it's important that the record reflect what they're about. I think I am moving through them fairly quickly, and there actually isn't too many more to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Round up as quickly as you can, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to move from this Drago Letic case, the disciplinary proceedings in this case were commenced in February 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On 24 February a disciplinary sanction was imposed, his service was terminated. On the 29th of February he appealed but the appeal was refused, so that the decision became final --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you repeat the date that it became final.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the decision became final on 12 June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's move to the next entry against a Serb police officer. This is with regard to Drasko Acic. Can you tell us what SJB he worked for.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Drvar SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now let's move to the entry of Petko Djukic. Can you tell us what was the disciplinary violation of Mr. Djukic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petko Djukic worked at the Prnjavor SJB. On 8 September 1992 he failed to report for carrying out a task and disciplinary sanction was imposed, his service was terminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn now to page 58 of the B/C/S, page 12 of the English. And can you tell us very quickly which entries on this page were for acts of misconduct committed between April and December 1992 by Serb police officers?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
